climbing_route.label: The one and only easy gully through the summit rock band
climbing_route.notes: Stay climber's-left and gain the south ridge of Pt. 8373 on open heather, then locate what guidebook notes call 'the one and only easy gully' near 7,200-7,300 ft breaching the summit rock band. Genuine route-finding difficulty picking the correct gully/ridge above the basin — parties have gotten cliffed out searching for it.

climbing_route.label: Broken rock and lingering snow to the final ridge
climbing_route.notes: Contour broken rock and lingering snow to reach the final south/west ridge.

climbing_route.label: Final south/west ridge to the summit
climbing_route.notes: A short class 3 scramble along the final south/west ridge finishes on the summit.

climbing_route.label: Colchuck Glacier to Colchuck–Dragontail Col
climbing_route.notes: Ascend the glacier from its toe at roughly 6,600–6,800 ft to Colchuck–Dragontail Col (Colchuck Col/Banshee Pass, ~8,200 ft). The glacier is not significantly crevassed but is frequently icy by mid-to-late season, so crampons and an axe (and a rope if any crevasses/moats have opened) are standard; stay right of the main rockfall line coming off the surrounding faces, especially in the morning-warming window. This is also the descent for the other two routes here.

climbing_route.label: Blocky terrain from the col to the summit
climbing_route.notes: From the col, scramble northwest on blocky terrain to the summit (8,705 ft).

climbing_route.label: Initial couloir ice
climbing_route.notes: From the base of the Colchuck Glacier/moraine below Colchuck's northeast face, the route starts right of the Northeast Couloir: two 60m pitches of AI3 ice gain the initial couloir.

climbing_route.label: Snow trending up-left
climbing_route.notes: Several hundred feet of 50-60 degree snow trending up-left, then unconsolidated snow over rock.

climbing_route.label: Chimney
climbing_route.notes: A short traverse left into an M6 chimney.

climbing_route.label: Final snow/rock band to the north ridge notch
climbing_route.notes: A final steep snow/rock band gains the notch on the north ridge crest.

climbing_route.label: Bergschrund to the base of the couloir
climbing_route.notes: From the bench, cross or tunnel through the bergschrund — often the route's crux obstacle, overhanging and requiring a mixed traverse from the right in leaner years — to gain the base of the couloir/gully system just right of the Polish Route, near 8,000 ft. The bergschrund crossing should be done early before the north-facing slopes see any sun-warming, and this route/aspect avalanches after new snow. The approach text stops here: it does not describe the couloir above the base.

climbing_route.label: Bergschrund to the first ice pitch
climbing_route.notes: From the bench, gear up and cross the bergschrund, which guards the Polish Route directly: it is frequently large and overhanging and has required climbers to traverse right and tunnel through overhanging snow/ice to gain the first ice pitch. This aspect avalanches after new snow, so the bergschrund/lower-face should not be done after recent loading.

climbing_route.label: Continuous ice line up the north face
climbing_route.notes: The route climbs the obvious continuous ice line up the middle of Colfax's north face, just left of (and parallel to) the Cosley-Houston gully. The face is northwest-facing, so it holds ice longest in the shade of an early start but catches afternoon sun — be off the technical ground before then.

climbing_route.label: Colonial Glacier to the Colonial-Snowfield col
climbing_route.notes: From the flat 6,100 ft basin at the glacier toe, rope up for glacier travel and ascend the Colonial Glacier, trending southeast/east across the upper glacier to the Colonial-Snowfield col or the base of the historic Northeast Gully. Crevasses are usually well-bridged under seasonal snow but are present and have been reported as a hazard, along with cornices along the traverse toward the col that are invisible from camp below.

climbing_route.label: Loose gully from the col onto the West Ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the col, leave the ice for a loose gully leading up onto the West Ridge.

climbing_route.label: West Ridge to the summit horn
climbing_route.notes: The West Ridge is followed via Class 3-4 rock scrambling to the summit horn.

climbing_route.label: Southeast Glacier
climbing_route.notes: Loose Class 3 talus/scree approaches the glacier on the peak's east face; rope up for glacier travel, as there is real crevasse hazard on the much-diminished but still present Southeast Glacier, especially early in the season.

climbing_route.label: Loose gully to the notch
climbing_route.notes: Above the glacier a loose Class 3 gully gains a notch on the ridge's north side.

climbing_route.label: Steep snowfield/snow gully above the notch
climbing_route.notes: A steep snowfield/snow gully beyond the notch can require crampons and, if icy, a belay.

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.skip_reason: The approach text stops at the Cosho/Kimtah saddle (~7,830 ft) / col. Everything it describes — the gullies leading north from ~3,800 ft, the steep talus, grass and some solid rock, the bushwhacking and loose scree — it explicitly calls 'the crux of the approach', and the alternate high-camp variant likewise ends at the col. Nothing describes the climbing from the saddle to the summit.
